query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Modifying the feedstock particle size distribution from 15–45 μm to a range around 45–70 μm—coupled with optimized APS spray parameters—will yield a thicker, more continuous FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat while maintaining coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy feedstock currently having a 15–45 μm particle size distribution used in APS deposition.
generation.intervention: Adopt a modified feedstock with a larger particle size distribution (e.g., 45–70 μm) and recalibrate APS parameters (spray distance, plasma power, etc.) to ensure full melting and proper deposition.
generation.conditions: Atmospheric plasma spraying performed in an inert (or controlled) atmosphere with optimized parameters (spray distance, plasma power, and stand-off distance) that are specifically tuned to accommodate larger feedstock particles without excessive oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The increased molten mass per particle will generate thicker, well-flattened splats that, upon rapid quenching, coalesce more effectively into a continuous, dense deposit.
generation.mechanism: Larger feedstock particles inherently provide a greater volume of molten material per deposition event. When fully melted under optimized APS conditions, these particles form larger splats with enhanced inter-splat bonding, thus building up a thicker coating. Fine-tuning the spray parameters ensures complete melting and controlled deposition, preventing defects and minimizing oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention is expected to produce a bond coat with a thickness significantly exceeding the original 15–45 μm baseline while retaining microstructural integrity and low levels of as-sprayed oxidation, making it suitable for service in thermal barrier coating systems.
generation.baseline: Previous APS depositions using 15–45 μm feedstock yield a bond coat with insufficient thickness and related deposition challenges.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this method is bounded by the ability to achieve complete melting and uniform deposition of the larger particles under APS conditions; improper parameter settings could lead to partially melted particles or microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the thickness increase and the long‐term performance stability of the thicker coating require experimental validation; there is uncertainty regarding optimal process parameters for uniformly melting and depositing larger particles.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of APS coatings on identical substrates—one using the conventional 15–45 μm feedstock and another using the modified 45–70 μm feedstock—with all other spray parameters held constant (after necessary recalibration for the larger particles). Compare coating thickness, morphology, and oxidation levels.
measurements: Phase analysis and oxidation level assessment using XRD and SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating produced using the modified, larger feedstock does not show a statistically significant improvement in thickness (or if it exhibits unacceptable microstructural integrity flaws or increased oxidation compared to the baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, because of its appropriate particle size distribution and good flowability, the powder milled for 10 h was chosen as a feedstock to deposit a coating. Figure 8 shows the surface morphology of the APS AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA coating. From Figure 8a, it can be seen that the coating showed a rough morphology, which is usually observed on the surfaces of atmospheric plasma sprayed coatings []. It can be observed that at a higher magnification (Figure 8b), most of the splats were fully molten and well flattened, and the outlines of the flattened splats could be observed obviously. Some spherical and droplet-shaped particles with dimensions of less than 10 μm could also be found on the coating surface, which originated from the sputtering of the flying particles when impacting the already formed coating surface.

The SEM images (Figure 1) show that the coatings exhibit a splat morphology containing dark and light phases. This can be attributed to the melting of particles owing to the high temperature of the plasma torch while few particles that experience lower temperatures can be seen to exist in a partially molten state also adhere to the substrate. The SEM image also revealed that the resultant microstructure was homogenized and the coatings have well adhered to the substrate with little porosity. The coatings have an average thickness of 150~180 µm. An enlarged microstructural view of the as-sprayed coatings is shown in (Figure 2), it can be seen that few oxide splats (light grey), voids, micro-cracks, partially molten particles, and the lamellar structure were present same as reported earlier by Ang et al. [], but their ratio to the homogenized structure is negligible.

proposals.intervention: Integrate a co-axial inert gas (e.g., argon) shroud to the APS torch
proposals.conditions: Atmospheric plasma spraying with added co-flow of argon at optimized flow rates (e.g., 10–20 L/min) during deposition on pre-cleaned substrates at ambient to moderately preheated temperatures (<200 °C)
proposals.structural_mediator: Reduced in-flight oxidation and enhanced particle melting efficiency
proposals.mechanism: The co-axial argon shield minimizes exposure of molten HEA particles to ambient oxygen, thereby reducing premature oxide formation while enhancing rapid splat formation. With less oxidation, more fully molten particles adhere and coalesce effectively, increasing deposition efficiency and overall coating thickness.
proposals.predicted_outcome: A significant increase in coating build-up beyond the baseline 15–45 μm feedstock result, preserving coating integrity and maintaining a minimal as-sprayed oxide level under typical service conditions (thermal barrier coating systems operating ~600–1000 °C).
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By modifying the spraying atmosphere around the particle trajectories, this single intervention directly tackles the thickness shortfall via improved deposition efficiency without compromising the alloy's integrity or oxidation state.

proposals.intervention: Increase the plasma power and control the gas chemistry to elevate particle temperature during APS
proposals.conditions: APS with increased net heat input (e.g., 10–20% higher plasma power) coupled with a reduced oxygen partial pressure in the plasma flame (adjusting the H2/Ar ratios) while keeping substrate preheat below 200 °C
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced melting and splat formation of HEA particles
proposals.mechanism: Elevated plasma power ensures more complete melting of feedstock particles, leading to increased droplet spreading and better in-flight cohesion upon impact. Adjusting gas chemistry minimizes oxidation risk while allowing the necessary thermal energy to drive denser deposit formation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: A thicker, more cohesive bond coat than the original 15–45 μm baseline, with minimal oxidation-related defects and improved adhesion suitable for high-temperature TBC service.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention improves the melting and deposition efficiency of particles, thereby overcoming the thickness shortfall while preserving the alloy’s microstructural integrity and resistance to oxidation.

proposals.intervention: Modify the feedstock particle size distribution to shift toward larger particles (e.g., 45–70 μm) while optimizing spray parameters
proposals.conditions: APS deposition using an adjusted feedstock where the median particle size is increased, with the spray distance and plasma parameters tuned to fully melt the larger particles under controlled atmosphere conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Increased molten mass per particle leading to thicker splats and improved inter-splat bonding
proposals.mechanism: Larger feedstock particles deliver a higher volume of material per droplet, which upon full melting and rapid quenching, coalesce into thicker layers. With careful control of spray parameters, the splats flatten adequately without excessive oxidation, ensuring a continuous, dense deposit.
proposals.predicted_outcome: An overall bond coat thickness exceeding the original target of 15–45 μm, with enhanced layer continuity and minimal oxidation, thereby improving its performance in thermal barrier coating systems.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By altering feedstock size, this single intervention increases the deposited material’s volume per pass, directly counteracting the thickness limitation while retaining coating integrity and low oxidation.

proposals.intervention: Preheat the substrate to an optimized temperature (e.g., 300 °C) prior to deposition
proposals.conditions: APS processing where the substrate is uniformly preheated to around 300 °C in an inert atmosphere immediately before deposition, maintaining controlled plasma conditions to avoid excessive oxidation
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced splat spreading and bonding at the interface
proposals.mechanism: Substrate preheating reduces the thermal gradient between the molten droplets and the substrate, promoting improved splat flattening and intersplat cohesion. This enhanced adhesion facilitates the building up of thicker layers while the inert atmosphere and controlled plasma settings help to curtail in-spray oxidation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: A robust, thicker deposition exceeding the nominal 15–45 μm obtained with cold substrates, ensuring improved bond coat durability and sustained integrity under service conditions of elevated temperatures in TBC systems.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: Preheating the substrate is a single, controllable parameter that enhances deposition efficiency and layer build-up by promoting better splat bonding, directly addressing the thickness shortfall without increasing oxidation.

critiques.addresses_problem: The proposal tackles the thickness shortfall by enhancing splat spreading and bonding, which directly contributes to building up the layer thickness.
critiques.constraints: It respects the constraints by keeping the process within APS parameters and using an inert atmosphere to limit oxidation, though careful control of the preheat temperature is essential to avoid any thermal damage to the substrate.
critiques.physical_soundness: The physics is sound: reducing the thermal gradient between molten droplets and the substrate can promote better spreading and inter-splat cohesion.
critiques.feasibility: The method is well established in thermal spray practices and is feasible with available equipment for controlled substrate preheating.
critiques.evidence: No explicit literature record IDs were provided; however, similar substrate preheating strategies have been reported in thermal spray studies.
critiques.main_risk: The key risk is that the increase in coating thickness may be marginal if the preheating does not sufficiently lower the thermal gradient, or if too high a temperature leads to inadvertent oxidation or substrate effects.
critiques.fix: Introduce an integrated thermocouple or infrared sensor feedback loop to precisely optimize and stabilize the substrate preheat temperature.

critiques.addresses_problem: By shifting the particle size distribution toward larger feedstock particles, this direction attempts to overcome the thickness shortfall by depositing more material per particle.
critiques.constraints: It meets the constraints by proposing optimized spray parameters to ensure complete melting and minimal oxidation, though care must be taken that the larger particles do not compromise coating integrity.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically reasonable, as larger particles provide greater mass and, when fully melted, lead to thicker splats and an increased deposit build‐up.
critiques.feasibility: Modifying feedstock size and tuning spray parameters are common practices in APS processes, making the approach feasible.
critiques.evidence: Although no specific literature records were provided, similar approaches to increase coating thickness via feedstock optimization have been noted in thermal spray research.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is incomplete melting or inconsistent deposition of larger particles if plasma parameters are not optimally recalibrated, which might lead to defects or uneven coating microstructure.
critiques.fix: Perform detailed parameter optimization studies to ensure that the larger particles are fully melted without sacrificing coating uniformity or oxidation control.

critiques.addresses_problem: The intervention focuses on limiting in-flight oxidation to enhance particle melting and deposition efficiency, indirectly supporting increased coating thickness.
critiques.constraints: It respects the constraints by using a co-axial inert gas shroud to reduce oxidation, though the effect on the overall thermal profile and splat formation must be carefully managed.
critiques.physical_soundness: Reducing oxidation and protecting molten droplets is a physically sound approach; however, the impact of an added gas shroud on the plasma plume dynamics must be considered.
critiques.feasibility: Integrating a co-axial inert gas shroud is feasible with APS equipment, but it requires precise control of the shroud gas flow rates.
critiques.evidence: No direct literature record IDs were provided; similar techniques have been explored to control oxidation during spraying in other systems.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that the inert shroud could disturb the plasma dynamics, possibly reducing particle velocities or altering the temperature profile, which might negatively affect deposition efficiency.
critiques.fix: Calibrate and optimize the inert gas flow rate to ensure it protects the particles without adversely disturbing the plasma plume characteristics.

critiques.addresses_problem: Increasing plasma power and modifying gas chemistry directly addresses the thickness shortfall by enhancing particle melting and promoting better splat adhesion.
critiques.constraints: It aligns with the process constraints by controlling the oxygen partial pressure to limit oxidation, although care is required to prevent excessive thermal input that may damage the substrate or alter the microstructure.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically plausible, as higher particle temperatures should improve melting and spreading, but must be balanced against the risk of thermal stresses.
critiques.feasibility: Enhanced plasma power and gas chemistry adjustments are established modifications in APS and are generally feasible with available technology.
critiques.evidence: No explicit literature records were cited, yet similar modifications in plasma spray processes have been documented to improve deposition characteristics.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the increased plasma power could lead to excessive thermal input, potentially causing substrate damage or inducing unwanted thermal stresses in the coating.
critiques.fix: Implement real-time thermal monitoring and feedback control during the process to ensure that plasma power increases do not compromise the substrate or coating integrity.

decision.rationale: Direction B directly targets the thickness shortfall by increasing the mass delivered per particle via a shift in the feedstock size distribution. Although there is a risk of incomplete melting or uneven deposition, this risk can be mitigated by detailed parameter optimization (the suggested fix). This approach directly increases the deposited material volume per pass while still preserving coating integrity and low oxidation, and it operates within the established APS framework, as supported by prior thermal spray research.
